legal-1750.intro: One of the oldest traps, said to date from Paris in 1750: White sacrifices the queen to checkmate with three minor pieces. Black loses because he only thinks about pinning the knight.
legal-1750.note5: The bishop eyes f7, the weakest point in Black's camp.
legal-1750.note6: It pins the f3 knight to the queen: it looks like a natural move.
legal-1750.note8: A mistake: Black doesn't notice that the pinned knight can still capture on e5.
legal-1750.note9: The sacrifice: the knight takes the pawn and leaves the queen hanging. If Black captures it, the king is left without defenders.
legal-1750.note11: The check forces the king to move and frees the d5 square.
legal-1750.note13: Checkmate: the king is boxed in by his own pieces, with the bishop and knights closing around him.
immortal-1851.intro: Anderssen gives up a bishop, two rooks and the queen to attack the black king, and wins with the few minor pieces he has left.
immortal-1851.note3: The King's Gambit: a pawn in exchange for development and an open center.
immortal-1851.note5: The Bishop's Gambit: White heads straight for f7.
immortal-1851.note6: The check takes away White's right to castle.
immortal-1851.note21: The rook on g1 looks out of play but will be one of the victims of the attack.
immortal-1851.note33: Anderssen doesn't defend the rook on a1: he keeps attacking the king.
immortal-1851.note35: Black can take two rooks, but meanwhile the net around his king tightens.
immortal-1851.note37: A pawn move that captures nothing: White prefers the attack to material.
immortal-1851.note43: The queen sacrifice: the black knight is forced to take her.
immortal-1851.note45: Checkmate: bishop and knights working together are enough, even though Black has far more material.
evergreen-1852.intro: A classic of the Evans Gambit: Anderssen opens the center, sacrifices a rook and then the queen with two checks in a row, and finishes with a bishop checkmate.
evergreen-1852.note7: The Evans Gambit: a pawn offered to gain tempi and build a big center.
evergreen-1852.note21: The bishop on a3 keeps Black from castling kingside.
evergreen-1852.note33: The knight jumps in with check: Black has to open the g-file.
evergreen-1852.note39: The rook sacrifice: the black knight is forced to capture and abandons the defense of d7.
evergreen-1852.note41: The queen sacrifice: the black king is forced to take her.
evergreen-1852.note43: The bishop's checks drive the black king toward f8, where checkmate is waiting.
evergreen-1852.note47: Checkmate: the bishop on e7 is protected by the f6 pawn.
opera-1858.black: Duke of Brunswick and Count Isouard
opera-1858.intro: Morphy plays from a theater box against two noblemen consulting together. He develops his pieces faster, then sacrifices the queen for a rook checkmate.
opera-1858.note7: Morphy opens the center: Black takes the knight but falls behind in development.
opera-1858.note13: A double threat: the queen attacks b7 and f7.
opera-1858.note17: The bishop pins the f6 knight: any move by it would put the queen in danger.
opera-1858.note19: A sacrificed knight opens the b-file and the bishop's check.
opera-1858.note23: Queenside castling brings the rook into play on the d-file.
opera-1858.note25: The rook takes the pinned knight: Black has to recapture.
opera-1858.note31: The queen sacrifice: the knight has to take her, and then checkmate is unavoidable.
opera-1858.note33: Checkmate: the rook on d8 is protected by the one on d1.
reti-tartakower-1910.intro: An eleven-move game: White sacrifices the queen to uncover a double check and delivers mate with the bishop.
reti-tartakower-1910.note9: The queen on d3 prepares the d-file: it looks like just a way to protect the knight.
reti-tartakower-1910.note15: White castles queenside and puts the rook behind the queen.
reti-tartakower-1910.note16: Black takes the knight and doesn't see the threat.
reti-tartakower-1910.note17: The sacrifice: the queen goes to d8 with check and the king is forced to take her.
reti-tartakower-1910.note19: Double check: the bishop and the rook give it together, so the king has to move.
reti-tartakower-1910.note21: Checkmate: the bishop on d8 is protected by the rook on d1.
capablanca-burn-1911.intro: A game from the book “Chess Fundamentals” (1921), where Capablanca annotates it for his students. Black loses time in development, Capablanca wins a pawn and then calmly carries it to victory, never giving Black a chance to attack. The comments retell his ideas in our own words.
capablanca-burn-1911.note9: Simple, solid development. Capablanca says he played it often back then because he didn't know many opening variations.
capablanca-burn-1911.note22: The bishop makes room for the queen, but according to Capablanca Be6 was better: it develops a piece and threatens Bc4.
capablanca-burn-1911.note28: A mistake: Black should first have traded the bishop for the knight that is about to arrive on d5.
capablanca-burn-1911.note29: The knight jumps to d5 and attacks the queen. The black knight on f6 is pinned by the bishop on g5.
capablanca-burn-1911.note33: White attacks the b5 pawn. Black can no longer avoid losing a pawn.
capablanca-burn-1911.note41: White has an extra pawn and all his pieces ready, while Black is still behind in development.
capablanca-burn-1911.note43: The knight heads for f5 and threatens Qh8+ and Nf5+. Black has to offer a queen trade, and any danger to the white king disappears.
capablanca-burn-1911.note61: The pawn drives the knight away from f4. Black has isolated pawns that have to be defended with pieces.
capablanca-burn-1911.note88: Black gives the rook for the knight, but the white kingside pawns are too strong.
capablanca-burn-1911.note91: The pawn reaches g6 and can't be stopped anymore: Black resigns.
capablanca-teichmann-1913.intro: From the book “Chess Fundamentals” (1921). From the opening on, Capablanca aims to leave Black with an isolated pawn on d5. Then he wins a pawn and wins the endgame with precise moves, even with bishops of opposite colors. The comments retell his ideas in our own words.
capablanca-teichmann-1913.note17: A move Capablanca invented during the game: it's a normal developing move and goes against no principle, so it can't be bad.
capablanca-teichmann-1913.note26: Black recaptures with the knight, but his pawn on d5 stays isolated: it will be the target for the whole game.
capablanca-teichmann-1913.note34: Black wants to trade queens to keep the two bishops. It's a mistake: the bishop on b7 is shut in behind the d5 pawn.
capablanca-teichmann-1913.note37: The knights move in a chain: one is always on d4 or ready to go there.
capablanca-teichmann-1913.note39: The knight attacks the bishop on e7. Capablanca writes that he doesn't see a good defense for Black.
capablanca-teichmann-1913.note45: The black knight on f6 is pinned. White threatens to bring the king to the center and Black can only wait.
capablanca-teichmann-1913.note47: White takes the h6 pawn: Black gave it up to free the knight.
capablanca-teichmann-1913.note57: The rook takes the c-file, the only open one.
capablanca-teichmann-1913.note62: Almost forced: otherwise the white king gets to d4, then c5, and eats the queenside pawns.
capablanca-teichmann-1913.note75: The bishop on g7 defends the d4 pawn. Now the white king can come in through f4 and Black resigns.
marshall-capablanca-1918.intro: From the book “Chess Fundamentals” (1921). Marshall wins a pawn, but the black rook on the seventh rank and the bishop on the long diagonal are worth more. Capablanca calls it an endgame to study very carefully. The comments retell his ideas in our own words.
marshall-capablanca-1918.note14: One of the oldest defenses against the Queen's Gambit: Black trades a few pieces to get room.
marshall-capablanca-1918.note24: The key to this defense: the bishop will go to the long diagonal without creating weaknesses. Developing it is Black's hardest problem.
marshall-capablanca-1918.note30: The knight attacks e4 and prepares the capture on d5: the position opens up.
marshall-capablanca-1918.note35: Marshall's surprise: if the black queen takes on a2, the rook goes to a1 and the queen is trapped.
marshall-capablanca-1918.note36: Perhaps the only good move: the queen offers a trade and Black is at least equal.
marshall-capablanca-1918.note40: The rook on the seventh rank is worth more than the pawn Black has lost.
marshall-capablanca-1918.note41: A misjudgment: White thinks he is better because he has an extra pawn. With Ne7+ he could have drawn.
marshall-capablanca-1918.note44: The pawn prevents f4. The white knight is almost pinned: if it moves, the black rook takes on e5.
marshall-capablanca-1918.note48: Better than taking pawns: the rook threatens to go to g6 and forces White to defend the knight.
marshall-capablanca-1918.note56: Look at the white pieces: they can't move without losing something.
marshall-capablanca-1918.note60: Another waiting move: White has to move and so worsens his position.
marshall-capablanca-1918.note62: Now the knight can't move: after h2+ the king takes the pawn, then Rh6+, Kg1 and Rh1 is mate.
marshall-capablanca-1918.note78: The black pawn on h2 is about to become a queen: White resigns.
byrne-fischer-1956.intro: Fischer is thirteen. After a queen sacrifice in return for a rook, a bishop and a pawn, his pieces dominate the board and Byrne can't avoid checkmate.
byrne-fischer-1956.note22: The knight attacks the queen and the knight on c3.
byrne-fischer-1956.note32: The rook check forces the king to move: from here Black has the initiative.
byrne-fischer-1956.note34: The move that made the game famous: the bishop on e6 offers the queen in return for an irresistible attack.
byrne-fischer-1956.note36: Black takes the bishop with check.
byrne-fischer-1956.note38: Repeated knight checks follow: the white king goes back and forth while Black collects material.
byrne-fischer-1956.note82: Checkmate: the rook on c2 is protected by the bishop and the knight covers b1 and d1, so the king has no escape.
kasparov-topalov-1999.intro: Kasparov sacrifices a rook and drags the black king from its home all the way to a4, in an attack that lasts about twenty moves.
kasparov-topalov-1999.note47: The rook sacrifice: White gives a rook to break the shelter around the black king.
kasparov-topalov-1999.note49: The second rook comes in with check: the black king can no longer go back.
kasparov-topalov-1999.note52: The black king is forced to take the knight and ends up on a5.
kasparov-topalov-1999.note53: The pawn gives check and pushes the king toward a4.
kasparov-topalov-1999.note59: The rook takes the bishop: White is winning material with the attack still going on.
kasparov-topalov-1999.note71: A quiet move: the bishop on f1 prepares the decisive threat Rd7.
